nap-18011109-30: Frenchmen, yours at last entire, this peace earned by such long generous efforts! The Amiens peace is won by your sacrifices.
nap-18011202-31: I tell montchoisy Paris disowns the Helvetic government. The Swiss puppet regime has no French backing.
nap-18011204-32: I citizen sage reports volta's hard case at Paris. The scientist's situation is reviewed.
nap-18020202-30: I Citizen Lebrun leaves tonight for Turin, delivering the enclosed to General Jourdan without stopping. The courier rides through the night.
nap-18020202-31: I hasten to Tell Your Holiness the Cisalpine Republic's affairs are arranged. The Italian Sister Republic is settled.
nap-18020202-32: General Silly reports Your Majesty's welcome to 300 French forced by sea onto Sicily. The Neapolitan king shows hospitality to our castaways.
nap-18020202-33: Your 12 Pluviose letter received. All moves at Amiens. Eight days more or less are now indifferent. The peace negotiations proceed at their own pace.
nap-18020205-34: I the minister proposes confirming fournier's hussar majority, lacking two years' grade. The promotion is justified by merit.
nap-18020206-35: I Article 1: memoirs, plans, drawings, all science and arts results of the Egypt expedition, shall be published at government expense. The Egyptian legacy is preserved for posterity.
nap-18020207-36: I Citizen Lauriston goes to Brest, waiting bouvet's squadron's sailing. The diplomat awaits the fleet.
nap-18020210-37: Glad to read you firmly constituted. You are a small state; live tranquil; shun faction. Lucca's independence depends on unity.
nap-18020607-81: A Barbary ship has been blockading a dozen Ligurian vessels at St. Tropez, and the Maritime Prefect has done nothing to disengage the port. It is a dishonour to the Republic that these Barbary wretches should insult our Coasts.
nap-18020906-81: I send you a note forwarded by the Inspector general of Gendarmery concerning the Bishop of Rennes.
nap-18021202-38: I Piedmont's church affairs need settling. If France has a Bishop per two departments, six may stay in Piedmont. The ecclesiastical map is redrawn.
nap-18021202-39: I report on wood-cutting bills as paper money. The forest revenue is audited.
nap-18021202-40: I direct only Germinal and Messidor timber receipts to fund Year XI; the rest to Year XII.
nap-18021202-41: I Tell General Brune to demand instant restitution of citizen ruffin's ship, seized by djezzar-pasha. The corsair's prize must be returned.
nap-18021204-42: I Duroc gives beauvoisin all his ambigu plus the ivernois pamphlet. The Press materials are distributed.
nap-18021207-43: I order Ré, Oléron and Sainte-Marguerite to hold all sentenced deportees. The island prisons receive the condemned.
nap-18021210-44: Deputies, your fatherland is critical. Moderation, prudence, sacrificed passions alone can save it. Switzerland's survival depends on restraint.
nap-18021210-45: I order plans for Quiberon, belle-ile and Boulogne batteries. The coastal defences are planned.
nap-18030203-46: Read the enclosed report. 'Liquidation of newly created pensions' means nothing to me. The pension accounts are opaque.
nap-18030203-47: I the 1,200 sailed from Havre, dunkerque ready, three Toulon expeditions: troops arriving together. The colonial convoys sail in coordination.
nap-18030204-48: Glad of Fort Dauphin retaken; take directly my full confidence and approval of vigorous measures. Rochambeau earns my trust.
nap-18030205-49: I fifteen thousand men shipped or shipping to saint-domingue. Combine now a 6,500 expedition. The colony receives massive reinforcements.
nap-18030208-50: I order the brisgau commander to receive two Austrian companies. The border garrison accepts the enemy detachment.
nap-18030208-51: My trust in your great talents bids me ask an elementary mathematics work for the national lycees. Haüy, write the textbook for the new schools.
nap-18030209-52: I the negre telemague thanks the first Consul for the cap mayoralty, protesting devotion to the Republic. The black mayor pledges loyalty.
nap-18030210-53: I Madame de staël, forbidden Paris, reaches melun the. Order police to turn her straight back. The exile is enforced at the gates.
nap-18030501-01: Your letter reached me at the Malmaison. I desire that the conference should not degenerate into a conversation. Show yourself cold, haughty, and even somewhat proud.
nap-18030623-24: I have received your letter, good little Josephine. I perceived with sorrow that you suffered from the journey. But a few days of repose will do much for you. I am very well.
nap-18030701-25: I have received your letter of the of. You do not speak of your health, or of the effect of the baths. I see that you intend to be on your return in eight days. That will afford great pleasure to your Friend, who wearies of being alone.
nap-18030801-02: Irish affairs move me to order secret talks with the United Irish chiefs in Paris. Offer them twenty-five thousand men, forty thousand muskets, guns and powder, and pledge no peace with England till Ireland stands free, if twenty thousand join us on landing.
nap-18030901-03: I return you the despatch from Madrid of the Fructidor. I am surprised that we have no other news. Make out a list of all the complaints we have against Spain, so that we may have materials ready in the event of requiring them.
nap-18031110-04: I return you your despatches, Citizen minister. Tell Citizen Laforest that I have read his despatch with great interest. It will be well to warn the Turkish ambassador that the English, who evidently encourage the Beys, intend to seize upon Egypt.
nap-18031112-05: Citizen general, I have received your letter, and have given orders for hoods to be served out to all the men forming part of the expedition to Ireland, of which you shall have the command. Affairs are settled with Spain and Portugal. Measures have been taken against desertion.
nap-18040101-34: My Friend, I have not received any news from you for several days; I should, however, have been glad to know what effect the waters have had, and how you pass your time. I have been here for the last week, and intend going tomorrow to Boulogne.
nap-18040214-06: For the last week we have been in pursuit of forty brigands composed of Georges and his band, who disembarked at three different places. Another band is to disembark; we have arrested all the men who were to make signals. Savary awaits them at Biville.
nap-18040301-81: You have no doubt heard that Pichegru was arrested yesterday. He was unable to make use of his pistols or of his sabre. He fought with his fists for half an hour with three or four gendarmes. The pleasure experienced by the people of Paris at this arrest does them credit.
nap-18040310-07: I the due d'enghien is to be taken to the castle of Vincennes, where arrangements have been made for his reception. The first Consul desires that the name of this prisoner, and everything concerning him, may be kept secret. He travels under the name of Plessis.
nap-18040410-08: I thank your Holiness for having given a cardinal's hat to the Archbishop of Bologna. I have come to the determination to take into my own hands all that relates to the Concordat with the Italian Republic.
nap-18040510-09: Steube, the minister of Wirtemberg, is a downright fool, as ill-meaning as ignorant. If you can insinuate in a delicate manner that he ought to be recalled, that would please me. Write to General Lannes at Lisbon, and mention the matter to M.
nap-18040530-10: Send Hawkesbury's note to all my agents save Russia, Sweden, Denmark, Porte, with my gloss: gross as its insults run, contempt were my due reply, but England's open maxims overturn Europe's order and must be answered.
nap-18040610-11: This wretched Moreau trial keeps me from the camps. I hope it ends within days. Camp and Paris buzz of a continental war; that would be fatal, turning us from England. Woe to war-seekers! Germany, Austria, Prussia stand with us.
nap-18040712-12: I desire that you will give me by return of post some information on the subject of the family of the Elector of Bavaria, especially concerning His Daughter, and his intentions with regard to that young princess.
nap-18040721-13: Madam and dear Wife, for the last four days since I have been absent from you I have been constantly on horseback, and this exercise has not impaired my health. M. Maret tells me that you intend starting on Monday.
nap-18040803-201: My love, I hope to hear shortly that the waters have done you very much good. I am pained that you have met with so many annoyances. I desire that you should write me often. My health is very good, although I am a little fatigued.
nap-18040806-02: My love, I have been at Calais since midnight. I think of setting out this evening for Dunkirk. I am satisfied with what I see, and am in very good health. I hope that the waters may benefit you, as much as the bustle, the sight of camps, and the ocean have me.
nap-18040901-14: I d'oubril has gone. Although this departure is not good news, still it does not mean a rupture; but it is incalculable what may happen within two or three months. And on the same day Fouche was ordered not to allow any Russians to leave Paris without having paid their debts.
nap-18040910-15: Holy Father, restored faith has remade my people's morals. Crown my work: come anoint the first French Emperor yourself. Your hands lend heaven's light; our peoples draw the Almighty's blessing on our decrees.
nap-18040914-16: Everywhere my police farmers coin money from gaming tables. I mean the towns to profit instead; Bordeaux tables yield two hundred thousand francs for a bridge or canal. To Berthier: Ireland is decided.
nap-18040916-17: Sir, my Uncle and Cousin, General Cafferelli is the bearer of the enclosed letter for the Pope. The Holy father will travel in his own carriages to the foot of Mont Cenis; arrived there, my carriages will bring him on.
nap-18041001-18: My friend, I reach Treves as you reach St Cloud. Grant T no audience. See B only in public, never alone. Sign no marriage contract till I have signed. To Fouche: Boulogne prefecture burned days before the English tried our flotilla.
nap-18041006-202: My love, I have arrived at Treves. At the same hour you reach St. Cloud. I am well. Do not grant an audience to T. Refuse to see him. Do not receive B. except publicly. Do not give him a private audience.
nap-18041029-19: You will see in the Moniteur of tomorrow an account of an unheard-of attack by the English on four Spanish frigates. Have several articles inserted in the papers with the object of exciting France to war, and of indisposing as much as possible the other powers against England.
nap-18041110-20: Sir, my Brother, I received your Majesty's letter this evening, and was much touched by the expressions of confidence and friendship which it contained. My first movement after reading your letter was to give orders for the immediate release of M. Rumbold.
nap-18041203-179: Behold your colors! These eagles will always be your rallying point! They will always be where your Emperor may think them necessary for the defence of his throne and of his people.
nap-18041210-21: I write you this letter to make known my displeasure in that you have permitted the word 'supper' to be used in the invitations of Wednesday, since the hour for which they are issued is that of my dinner.
nap-18050102-180: My Brother: Called to the throne by Providence, by the suffrages of the Senate, of the people, and of the army, my first desire is peace. France and England, abusing their prosperity, may contend for ages. But I desire peace, and I hope that England will not refuse it.
nap-18050130-22: Most high, most excellent, most powerful, most magnanimous and invincible prince, great Emperor of the Mussulmans, Sultan Selim, in whom honour and virtue abound, our very dear and perfect friend, may God augment your grandeur and accord you a happy end.
nap-18050201-23: The present letter will be presented to your royal highness by General Junot, my ambassador.
nap-18050310-24: I a great many persons complain that classics are too dear. It would be well to appoint a commission to tax the price of books adopted by the lyceums at so much a page.
nap-18050401-25: Your courier tells me Dominica fell. My Toulon squadron sailed a fortnight ago with Lauriston's division; no news yet. England bleeds in India; Decaen arms the Mahrattas with guns and officers. A Walcheren venture is madness.
nap-18050410-26: I beg you will inform M. De Moustier that I cannot conceive how a man of so much judgment allows 30,000 Russians to alarm him for Prussia which has 300,000 men. The artillery, cavalry, and officers of the Prussian army are worth thirty times those of Russia.
nap-18050421-27: I forward you a report concerning Creusot. It is essential to keep up this establishment. It will not be well to purchase it; but I think it will be useful to give a fixed amount of orders, so that it may have a basis of operations, and be able to support itself. To M.
nap-18050506-181: Jerome fancies some weakness in me will indulge him. Having no father's rights, I bear no father's blind love; a father loves being blind, seeing himself in his son. I cannot be blinded where duty rules. Let him earn, not presume.
nap-18050506-28: Sir, my Brother-in-law and Cousin, what you write concerning the conclusion of a treaty of alliance between England and Russia is nonsense; it is entirely false. These reports, spread by the English so that they may for the moment escape from their difficulties, are unfounded.
nap-18050526-29: I want letters printed as from Petersburg: Frenchmen well used there, court and town for friendship, English greed blamed for the war, their coalition broken, Russia still.
nap-18050529-30: The people of Genoa appear to desire their union to France. The advantages of this union, and circumstances, are such as to induce me to pay no attention to the blustering of a few powers. In fact, this can excite the animadversion of England alone.
nap-18050601-31: As nothing would give me a better idea of the exact feeling of the court of Vienna than a negotiation with the view of exchanging a certain number of cordons of the legion of honour against Austrian cordons, write to M. de la Rochefoucauld to tell M.
nap-18050720-32: I think I ordered you to embark everything, for circumstances may present themselves at any moment. I wish you to embark the artillery, powder, and all the ammunitions, so that in twenty-four hours the whole expedition may start.
nap-18050727-33: I have directed M. Marescalchi to forward you a decree, ordering the Legislative body to terminate its sittings. My intention is that during my reign in Italy it shall not meet again. I had too good an opinion of the Italians.
nap-18050731-34: All the news I receive from Italy is warlike, and Austria no longer conceals her intentions. Prepare a note for M. de Cobentzel, let it be long, wily, argumentative, and in similar terms to the inclosed. The note drawn up by Talleyrand was approved of, and forwarded to Vienna.
nap-18050814-38: With thirty sail my admirals should not fear twenty-four English, or disband the navy. If Villeneuve idles at Ferrol past my deadline I call him the basest of men. London says Nelson roams far.
nap-18050901-182: Soldiers, the third coalition's war is opened. Austria crossed the Inn, broke treaties, drove our ally from his capital. You yourselves were forced to double-march to our frontiers. They forced this war on us; answer with the courage that ever marks French arms.
nap-18050901-39: I have arrived at Strasburg. All the army has passed the Rhine. The enemy is at the issues of the Black Forest. Our manoeuvres will soon commence. Do all you can to induce the nation to adopt the conscription.
nap-18051002-40: My brother, yours received. Prussia never cared about troops crossing Baireuth and Anspach; we crossed that country at will all last war. A month ago I promised to stand mid-Germany by early next month; with God's help I soon restore you to Munich.
nap-18051002-41: My good Josephine, I have fatigued myself more than was prudent. All day long for a whole week wet to the skin, and the feet cold, have made me rather unwell; but I have not been out to-day, and that has reposed me.
nap-18051023-203: The two last nights have rested me much, and I shall leave tomorrow for Munich. I send for M. de Talleyrand and M. de Maret to be near me. I shall see them but little. Talleyrand was then minister of Foreign affairs.
nap-18051101-43: I think there will be no inconvenience in your coming to meet me at the Abbaye de Moelk. You can pass by Braunau where you will see General Lauriston. The Emperor of Germany is still at Vienna. He has written me several letters, and would like to come to an arrangement.
nap-18051102-42: Sire, I send Savary, my aide, to greet your arrival. I charge him to avow my esteem and my hunger for chances to prove how I covet your friendship. Receive him with your famed kindness, and count me foremost among those who would please you.
nap-18051116-204: I write to M. D'Harville in order that you set out, and that you proceed to Baden, from thence to Stuttgard, and from there to Munich. You will give at Stuttgard the wedding present to the Princess Paul. It is sufficient that it cost fifteen to twenty thousand francs.
nap-18051202-44: My brother, yours received. Talks drag on; my army rests. Charles's host lies close. Likely, if peace lags, within weeks comes a stroke leaving Austria not a shadow of resource. I wait, ready.
nap-18051202-45: I have received your letter of the Nivose. The Emperor and Prince Charles have written to me. I shall have an interview with the archduke at three leagues from Vienna. I send you a copy of my letter to the Emperor, who has written to me in the most amiable manner.
nap-18051203-184: I am satisfied with you. In the battle of Austerlitz you have justified all that I expected from your intrepidity. You have decorated your eagles with immortal glory.
nap-18051203-205: I have dispatched Lebrun to you from the field of battle. I have beaten the Austrian and Russian armies commanded by the two Emperors. I am a little fatigued. I have bivouacked eight days in the open air, through some very cold nights.
nap-18051203-46: After manoeuvring for a few days I fought a decisive battle yesterday. I defeated the combined armies commanded by the Emperors of Russia and of Germany. Their force consisted of 80,000 Russians and 30,000 Austrians.
nap-18051205-206: I have concluded a truce. The Russians have gone home again. The battle of Austerlitz is the most glorious of all which I have gained.
nap-18051207-207: I have concluded an armistice. Before eight days, peace will be made. I hope to learn that you have arrived at Munich, in good health. The Russians have retired. They have sustained an immense loss; more than twenty thousand killed and thirty thousand taken.
nap-18051214-50: The Emperor of Germany asked for an interview, which I granted; it lasted from 2 till 4 P.M. I will tell you what I think of him when I see you. He wished to conclude peace on the spot.
nap-18051225-49: My Brother, I send you a letter for the minister of the treasury (M. Barbe-Marbois). You will read it, then seal it and hand it to him. I do not yet know whether it is incapacity or treason, but the coalition has had no more useful ally than this minister.
nap-18060112-52: You will stand near Rome within days. I send Dumas; Massena should be there. After brief rest count forty thousand in three corps: Massena strongest, St Cyr another, Regnier a six-thousand reserve. Befriend cold Regnier; he plans best.
nap-18060124-53: Occupy Frankfort with one division, levying nothing yet. Only with your whole corps united will you demand four millions for the Grand Army's chest. I decree victory beforehand, after the Convention's fashion.
nap-18060410-54: My Cousin, the affairs of Cattaro are not getting settled; however, I have decided to remain in Germany until I know how matters are likely to turn out. Keep an eye on the movements of the Austrians.
nap-18060422-55: My Brother, I see with pleasure that you have burned an insurgent village. I suppose that you allowed the soldiers to pillage it. That is the way in which villages which revolt should be treated. It is the right of war, and it is also a duty prescribed by policy.
nap-18060501-58: My sister, yours received. Exact no oaths from priests; it breeds trouble. Go your way; shut the convents. I published the Concordat at Lucca and the Pope meddled; my sharp note answered. What saves souls at Bologna saves at Lucca. Ask Pius if he takes me for a weak prince.
nap-18060510-56: After all the difficulties in the way of constructing the Arc de Triomphe on the site of the Bastille, I consent to its being constructed at the gate of Chaillot, at l'Etoile [where it now stands].
nap-18060510-57: My son, Lemarois should be at Ancona by now; I give him my Papal States troops. He is an old trusted aide, witness of my midnight civil wedding to Josephine before a sleepy mayor. I trust him fully.
nap-18060510-59: I am not at all surprised that you are satisfied with Marshal Jourdan. I was equally satisfied with him in the administration of Italy; he is an upright, active, and methodical man. I do not see why you leave Massena at Capua.
nap-18060513-60: I see with pleasure the energy which you display in governing. The forty-four individuals condemned to death and to the galleys is a salutary measure, which will serve as an example, and will check those who desire to indulge in their natural inconstancy.
nap-18060516-61: My Cousin, I have re-called you from Rome because it is not in accordance with my dignity that you should remain at so ill-conducted a court which does all it can to annoy me, and which I shall be constrained to punish sooner or later.
nap-18060610-62: I asked you for a note on the forces of Prussia. The information contained in the letters of Laforest is not what I want. I require to know the general situation of the army of the king of Prussia.
nap-18060610-63: Lord Yarmouth has arrived, with full powers from the king of England to sign peace. We should be tolerably well agreed but for Sicily. The English will recognise you as king of Naples, but, as you have not taken Sicily, they cannot recognise you there.
nap-18060610-64: I see with pleasure that you are satisfied with the Dutch. The pretensions of your finance minister are out of the question. My expenses are heavy, and I cannot aid you as I should like. As long as the war lasts I shall be obliged to keep up my army.
nap-18060619-65: Inform M. Alquier that I regard the Pope from a temporal and from a spiritual point of view. As a temporal prince he forms part of my confederation, whether he likes it or no.
nap-18060702-66: We have no news from General Regnier. The art of war about which every one speaks is a difficult art; you have not a man in your council who understands the first notions of it. I have concluded peace with Russia (treaty not ratified). Negotiations are going on with England.
nap-18060726-67: It is my intention to organise nine metropolitan seminaries without delay. Present me a report on the number of priests necessary.
nap-18060807-69: I send you a letter, which will make you thoroughly acquainted with that scamp Lucchesini. My opinion was formed long ago with respect to that wretch. He has continually deceived you, because I have long perceived that nothing is more easy.
nap-18060810-70: My Son, I send you a copy of the catechism, which has been adopted for France; it would be a good thing if it could be adopted for Italy without inconvenience. But it is a delicate matter, and you must be very circumspect. Consult the minister of worship.
nap-18060814-68: My Son, I thank you for what you say about my fete day. Affairs are getting settled. I will soon send you instructions for your voyage to Paris. I know that you wish to come here. You will see the queen of Holland. We will keep the princess until after her confinement.
nap-18060830-71: My daughter, yours pleased me. Trust my love. Guard yourself in your state, and give us no daughter, if you please! I could give a recipe, did you believe: a glass of pure wine daily.
nap-18060907-73: I see with surprise that the chief of the staff dares to correspond with the enemy without your permission. General Caesar Berthier is then ignorant of his duty! The reply of Sidney Smith is impertinent, as is everything which emanates from that officer.
nap-18061001-77: I have received the letter of your Royal Highness. I was much touched by the pOSITION of Madame de Hatzfeld. I convinced her that her husband was guilty, and that, according to the laws of war, he ought to be executed. However, I spared him even the disagreeableness of a trial.
nap-18061014-75: Immediately after the battle of Jena the king of Prussia sent me an aide-de-camp with a letter. Today he sends me the Marquis de Lucchesini. I have ordered him to remain at the outposts, and I have sent Duroc to know what he wants.
nap-18061015-188: Captive officers after Jena: I know not why I war with your sovereign, a wise, peaceable prince I respect. I would free your country from degrading vassalage to Prussia. Lay down ancient hatreds; France offers friendship.
nap-18061015-76: My Friend, I have manoeuvred finely against the Prussians. Yesterday I gained a great victory. They had 150,000 men. I took 30,000 prisoners, 100 guns and standards. I was in presence and close to the king of Prussia; I nearly captured him and the queen.
nap-18061023-208: I have received many letters from you. I can write you but a word. My Affairs are very prosperous. I shall be tomorrow at Potsdam, and the at Berlin. I am remarkably well; fatigue refreshes me.
nap-18061025-78: I have crushed the Prussian monarchy; I shall crush the Russians if they arrive. I no longer fear the Austrians. I shall not ask you for any troops; I have no need of them. If, however, you could send me some cavalry, do so.
nap-18061102-209: I have received your letter of the of. We have here superb weather. You will see by the bulletin that we have taken Stettin. It is a very strong place.
nap-18061121-79: I am at Kustrin in order to make some reconnaissances. I shall see, in two days, if you can come. Hold yourself in readiness. I hope that the queen of Holland will be of the party. It is two o'clock in the morning. I have just risen; this is the custom of war.
nap-18061127-80: I am going to take a town in Poland. This is the first town. This evening I shall be at Posen. After that I will call you to Berlin, so that we may arrive there on the same day. My health is good. The weather is rather bad; it has been raining for three days.
nap-18061201-81: I have a circular written, and take measures so that, throughout the extent of the empire, all letters coming from England, or written in English and by Englishmen, be seized. This is most important, as it is absolutely necessary to isolate England.
nap-18061201-82: Prussia, which had formed a league with Russia, has disappeared. I have destroyed her armies, and am master of her strong places. My armies are upon the Vistula, and Warsaw is in my power.
nap-18061202-210: Today is the anniversary of Austerlitz. I have been to a ball given by the city. It rains. I am well. I love you, and long for you. My troops are at Warsaw. It is not yet cold. All the Polish ladies are French, but there is only one woman for me.
nap-18061214-83: My Friend, I am starting for Warsaw. I shall be back in a fortnight, when I hope I shall be able to send for you. However, I should see you return to Paris, where you are desired, with pleasure. You know that I depend upon events. All my affairs are going on well.
nap-18061215-211: My love, I leave immediately for Warsaw. In a fortnight I shall be on my return. I hope that then I shall be able to send for you. Nevertheless, should there be still delay, I should see you with pleasure return to Paris, where you are desired.
nap-18061220-212: I have received no news from you, my love. I am very well. I have been at Warsaw for two days. My Affairs go on well. The weather is very mild, and even a little humid. We have as yet had scarcely any frost. It is the weather of. Adieu, my love.
nap-18061229-213: I can write you but a word, my love. I am in a wretched barn. I have beaten the Russians. I have taken thirty pieces of cannon, their baggage, and have made six thousand prisoners. But the weather is frightful. It rains; we have mud to the knees.
nap-18061231-84: I laughed heartily on receiving your last letter. You have formed an idea of the belles of Poland which they do not deserve. I received your letter in a wretched barn, having mud, wind, and straw for my bed. Tomorrow I shall be at Warsaw.
nap-18070102-85: I think that you have done wrong to create marshals, which has the inconvenience of costing money, and of giving men who have done little great pretensions. Do you think that a French general of Division would be commanded by a Dutch marshal?
nap-18070107-03: My love, I am deeply affected by all that you say to me; but the season cold, the roads wretched, the region unsafe, I cannot consent to expose you to such perils and dangers. Return to Paris, to pass the winter there.
nap-18070107-88: I have received your letter of the, and thank you for all you say. I am aware of your attachment, which I greatly prize. What are you doing in Paris? I have not heard that you gave a little ball during the Carnival.
nap-18070114-87: Turkey declared against Russia. A Tartar from Constantinople brings me prime news. A million comes to you from Turin. My health never stood better, whence, they tell me, I grow more gallant.
nap-18070114-91: I have received your letter of the. The affair of Hesse Cassel is terminated. It appears that it was the soldiery which wished to move.
nap-18070116-86: My good friend, I have received your letter of the; what you say of your grief gives me pain. Why these tears, this chagrin? I shall soon see you; do not doubt my sentiments; and if you wish to be still dearer to me exhibit greater strength of mind.
nap-18070118-214: I fear that you are greatly disappointed in view of our separation, which must yet be prolonged some weeks, and of your return to Paris. I expect of you more force of character. They tell me that you weep continually. Fie! How unbecoming that is.
nap-18070119-04: My love, I am in the receipt of your letter. I have smiled at your fear for my safety. I am in despair at the tone of your letters, and at what I hear of you. I forbid you to weep, to be melancholy and anxious; I wish that you may be cheerful, amiable, and happy.

nap-18110903-17: I beg that you will pay 2,500 francs a month to the ex-queen of Etruria, at her convent in Rome. The poor queen of Etruria, deprived of her kingdom, which was handed over by me to my Sister Eliza, was most cruelly treated.
nap-18111101-19: I return you the letters from Savona.
nap-18111231-20: I have just seen the porcelain service sent to the Empress as a new year's gift. It is very ugly. See that it be prettier another yEAR. Have a breakfast service made, and on each cup the portraits of the Empress and of the six princesses, my sisters and Sister-in-law.
nap-18120307-21: It will be necessary to send a courier to Comte Lauriston to-day. Do not speak to him about the espionage of Czernitchef, of which you are supposed to know nothing at present.
nap-18120406-22: I return you the letters of your Brother. Reply that cacao, sugar, and coffee are not English merchandise, and ought not to be burned. What ought to be burned are articles of English manufacture.
nap-18120616-23: I write to Marshal Ney that his corps is diverging from the route traced out for it, and commits devastation everywhere.
nap-18120618-81: I similar suspicions attach to the conduct of the captain of the danae who might have helped the Rivoli. The conduct of the post captain who was at lorient is sharply criticised; it is said that he might have succoured the two frigates. Make a report on these two affairs.
nap-18120701-25: Write to Marshal Ney that the situation of his army corps seems to me very alarming as regards his artillery. Without artillery his corps would be greatly compromised.
nap-18120702-24: Davoust fought at Mohilef; details still out. Bagration tried to ride over him and broke. An evening field-note says the foe beaten. Today our van took eight guns and seven hundred men. Russia lies at Vitebsk. Keep this to yourself; write nothing. Great events ripen.
nap-18120801-28: I have received your Calculation of Probabilities with pleasure. There was a time when I should have read it with interest; to-day I must confine myself to expressing the satisfaction which I experience every time that I see you bring out new works.
nap-18120802-26: I have received the portrait of the king, and find it very like him. It furnishes me with an opportunity, of which I avail myself with pleasure, of expressing my satisfaction with the care you take of him.
nap-18120807-27: I beg that you will see if the two or three hundred carts left behind at Wilna, exposed to the air, have been placed under cover in a church or an arsenal. If that has not yet been done the governor should see to it.
nap-18120829-29: We reached Viazma; the foe still melts toward Moscow. I wait word of two Russian divisions marching from Moldavia. I begged Austria to stiffen Schwartzenberg's horse with three thousand to cover his losses.
nap-18120907-91: Borodino: soldiers, the battle you craved is come. Victory rests with you; we need it. It brings full winter quarters and swift homecoming. I ask the impossible no longer, strike!
nap-18120920-92: Monsieur my brother: learning your Cassel minister's brother lingers in Moscow, I sent for him and spoke long. I bid him carry you my mind. War wastes both empires; I still prefer an understanding. Hear me through him.
nap-18121001-30: I repeat: Marchand gathers all sick and wounded to Mojafsk abbey with every cart and carriage; staff sees it done.
nap-18121107-31: I have just passed the Beresina, but the ice floating down that river makes the bridges very unstable. The army which was opposed to Schwartzenberg wished to dispute the passage; tonight it is concentrated on the right bank of the river at Borisoff.
nap-18121201-34: You must go to Berlin, and before leaving Wilna let me know how things are looking. You will find at Berlin a letter for the king of Prussia, and my instructions for yourself. You must wait at Berlin for orders and write to me every day. 266 Polish lancers formed his escort.
nap-18121210-33: I have received your letter of the. I see nothing very important in the Moniteur on the subject of Spain. The resistance of the castle of Burgos is a fine military affair, but it simply proves that forts are not to be taken without siege guns.
nap-18121214-32: I pause at Dresden to write you. Despite fatigue my health never was better. I left Lithuania after Beresina, leaving the Grand army to the king of Naples. In four days I reach Paris for the most urgent affairs.
nap-18130101-35: I received your letter. I see the army command in your hands with pleasure. I find the king of Naples extravagant; little more and I would have him arrested as an example. He is brave in Battle but devoid of combinations and moral courage. Employ Ney; you will need him.
nap-18130126-36: All your efforts must preserve Warsaw. Reports show the Russians on the Beresina thought themselves lost; but for Partouneaux wandering into their lines, Victor would have beaten them as we beat the admiral and crushed them.
nap-18130302-37: I received your letter from Leipsic. Send me news of Morand, even rumours. After York's treason, Prussia will not stay our ally long, though the issue is still undecided. I do not think she has as many troops as Regnier.
nap-18130312-38: It is unfortunate you do not see Magdeburg can only live by requisitions, authorised by war and practised since the world began; Italy in my last campaign, even Strasburg and Mayence lived so. Why not do for Magdeburg what I did for Mayence? Instead of energy you undo all.
nap-18130426-39: I do not intend you to send your police memoranda straight to the Empress. It has no advantage and many objections. She is too young to have her mind corrupted or disturbed by police details. Address such papers to me alone.
nap-18130504-40: Knowing your joy in my fortune, I announce Lutzen, which Providence gave my arms. Though I ordered all under fire myself, I came through untouched and hale. I hear daily from the Empress, my prime minister, to my full content.
nap-18130507-43: Send the enclosed to Serra at Prague. We reached Dresden; tomorrow the army crosses in pursuit. Tell Senft that to offend the confederation is war against me; my friendship made me patient till now, but the crisis lets you grant Saxony only six hours for satisfaction.
nap-18130510-41: We reached Dresden; I hold both banks and the Elbe strongholds. Likely I march into Silesia. Long disgraced, Fouche now gets my secret summons: as I enter Prussia I will set him over its government. Lutzen drove the foe over the river; let him come at once. Only the Regent knows.
nap-18130512-42: I gave battle to the Russo-Prussian army entrenched at Bautzen and Hochkirch, and Providence granted me victory. I tell you my health is excellent, counting on your interest.
nap-18130531-44: The Swedes having entered Hamburg, send me at once a declaration of war against Sweden. Their insolence must be answered without delay.
nap-18130531-45: I direct you: should the case of the queen of Sicily arise, treat her with the honours of her rank and utmost consideration; she is the Empress's grandmother and an unfortunate queen persecuted by the English.
nap-18130601-46: I saw with pleasure that amid political storms your feelings stayed unchangeable. Sweden's ill will comes from my refusal to join the spoliation of Norway.
nap-18130717-47: I hold the Bishop of Nantes the most enlightened priest of the empire, the finest Doctor of the Sorbonne. None was more steeped in the Gospel; none better honoured sovereigns' rights while rejecting Rome's monstrous abuses, which shed so much blood and schisms in ignorant days.
nap-18130801-50: Present me a plan for gratifying my actors, and tell Turenne to send them back to France by the twelfth. I wrote Savary on the crisis; see him. I hope to make Austria repent her folly and treason. Likely the foe denounces the armistice and Austria declares war on us.
nap-18130801-51: My minister will have told you Austria declared war. Her manifesto is empty; plainly she seizes the hour to recover influence. The Prague talks never happened; envoys never met. Spanish hopes and English intrigue did the rest. We fight soon.
nap-18130807-49: I told you Oudinot with Vandamme, Regnier and Padoue, eighty thousand men, debouches by Luckau and Bayreuth when the armistice breaks, to stand days from Berlin.
nap-18130817-48: I long thought Caulaincourt and Narbonne Let Metternich's honeyed style dupe them. The Austro-Russian terms were settled last winter, and I am sure the conditions for me were signed then.
nap-18130825-109: I received your letter. I see with pleasure that you are in good health. I spent days at Trianon and my health is good. Take care of yourself and write often. I think of you and send my love.
nap-18130826-52: I told you my plans yesterday. The whole foe appeared before Dresden and St Cyr feared attack; I go there myself. To divert them, debouch at once and fall on their rear today, crushing the division watching you.
nap-18130830-53: Alexander's host lies utterly beaten. I took thirty thousand men, scores of guns, thirty colours; twelve thousand wounded strew the villages. Vandamme smashed Wurtemberg's Russians and marches on. Austria's new levies melt half-naked and shoeless after days afield.
nap-18130901-55: Macdonald stands at Gorlitz; should he keep retiring I must aid him. The disaster to the first corps was unforeseeable: Vandamme posted no sentry and kept no reserve.
nap-18130902-54: Write Ney: Oudinot rashly ventured near Wittenberg, so Tauentzien and Cossack clouds cut Macdonald's communications. Few have less brains. march to Bayreuth by the sixth; thence three marches from Berlin, our link restored, and the capital can be struck within days.
nap-18131031-56: I arrived here. Sixty thousand Bavarians and Austrians at Hanau tried to cut me from France. I gave them a drubbing, taking guns, standards and six thousand prisoners. My health never was better; I go to Mayence.
nap-18131110-57: The English push on Bayonne opened my frontier; they already landed goods near St Jean de Luz. I suppose you moved your customs line; this deserves your attention. Bavaria urges Eugene to desert me as she did herself, but he reported and rejected it. I see Austria's hand.
nap-18131110-58: Burn Marracq castle and all my houses there should the English come, so they never sleep in my bed. To Fouche: hasten to Naples and press the king to march to the Po; tell the queen too, and keep the land from Austria's false promises and vile tongue. I doubt him deeply.
nap-18140102-59: I marched on St Dizier, held by the foe, and drove them out, taking guns and prisoners. Blucher with twenty-five thousand men reached Brienne today. I cut his communications, occupied Bar, and now pursue him. If he stands we fight at Brienne on the morrow.
nap-18140110-60: Garrison every place; recall Sebastiani and your horse for the Meuse, turning Blucher's right toward Namur. Marmont wheels round Metz; Ney and Victor bar the Vosges; Mortier holds Langres.
nap-18140201-61: What! Hours after your Spanish drafts arrived, still not afield! Brief rest sufficed me: I won Nangis with dragoons fresh from Spain who never unbridled. You plead your Nismes battalions want clothes and drill, poor excuses!
nap-18140202-62: The allies set the Chatillon congress to open within days: Cathcart for London, Stadion for Austria, Humboldt for Prussia, Razoumovsky for Russia. I shall be at Troyes tomorrow. To Caulaincourt: the foe behaves vilely; villagers flee to the woods.
nap-18140206-63: I marvel Suchet never sent the Lyons Troops I demanded; they should be here and I hear nothing. If he disobeyed on his own head he is most culpable. To Joseph I wrote: I meant to strike Alexander at Bar and beat him, but false moves spoiled it.
nap-18140207-66: I note your gains with pleasure; had they been more decisive we could have kept Italy. I crushed the Silesian army and began beating Schwartzenberg. In days I took tens of thousands of prisoners, generals, hundreds of officers and scores of guns.
nap-18140210-64: I just reached Nogent. After Montereau the foe fell back on Troyes in bulk; only frost letting them march cross-country saved their baggage and guns. At Montereau, Bray and Nogent they committed unspeakable horrors; Let Paris know. Austria's Emperor never left Troyes.
nap-18140214-65: I send word of Vauchamps. Blucher, cut off at Vertus, joined Kleist and a fresh Russian corps, twenty thousand men, and marched on Etoges while Marmont fell back.
nap-18140220-67: Bassano sends you the allied proposals. You will see your sermons are misplaced; I need no preaching to sign an honourable peace if possible. He sends too an intercepted Angouleme letter.
nap-18140303-68: Before fortifying Paris the plan must be settled; yours is too tangled, I demand simplicity. Complaints reach me that mayors and bourgeois stop the people defending themselves. I see the same in Paris.
nap-18140310-71: The army I beat at Craonne was Russian. It lost heavily and fell back on Laon, joined by Bulow, York and Kleist forming the Prussian army. Laon favours them; yesterday I only observed it. This army threatens Paris more than Schwartzenberg's. I move toward Soissons.
nap-18140314-69: I reached Rheims, held by St Priest with three Russian divisions and a Prussian one fresh from Stettin. I beat them, retook the town, twenty guns, much baggage, five thousand prisoners. St Priest is mortally wounded, struck, remarkably, by the same gunner who killed Moreau.
nap-18140315-70: Mortier writes the foe retreats in good order on Laon; I sent horse to follow. Send peasants to learn if they hold Craonne in force. Recruit the villages through the mayors, sending officers and men; many ruined peasants ask only to serve.
nap-18140320-72: Yesterday I crossed the Aube at Plancy and marched straight on Mery, carried by evening. Alexander was at Arcis; we nearly met face to face before he fled to Troyes, at once evacuated by his headquarters. The foe flies everywhere.
nap-18140323-73: Send a disguised gendarme to Metz, one to Bar, one to Nancy, with letters to the mayors. Tell them we march on the enemy's rear; the hour is come to rise as one, ring the tocsin, seize their commandants and agents, and fall on their convoys.
nap-18140404-95: The allied powers proclaim me the sole bar to peace in Europe. Faithful to my oath, I declare myself ready to leave the throne, to quit France, even to die for my country's welfare, inseparable from my son's rights and the Empress's regency. I make this sacrifice for France.
nap-18140405-90: Soldiers, yielding to the necessity that parts me from the brave French army, I carry the sure knowledge that you will justify, by the great services the country expects of you, the praise even our enemies cannot refuse you. I thank you for twenty years of glory.
nap-18140420-96: Soldiers of my Old Guard, I bid you farewell. For twenty years I marched with you on the road to honour and glory. In these last days, as in our prosperity, you stood as models of courage and fidelity. I shall remember you always.
nap-18140610-74: I appoint the mayor of Porto Longone warden of my palace there: warden, keeper, master of the wardrobe and of the gardens, at six hundred francs. As the theatre must come down One day, I will spend nothing needless on it.
nap-18140826-75: I asked you to Tell Pauline to leave her piano master behind and bring only a good singer and songstress; we already have a fine violinist and pianist here. One of my mules drowned for want of a small stable pump; have a spare one mended. Send off Beausset's courier with my word.
nap-18140901-76: Tell Pauline I got all the Naples letters, and I am hurt mine reached her opened, as if I were a prisoner; I call such handling ridiculous and insulting. Thank Bertrand for the pamphlets, for and against; I will read them all one day.
nap-18150301-78: Plan me Soissons, La Fere, Chateau Thierry against surprise. Angouleme showed at Avignon; Paris events, I judge, forced him back. Spain at his rear still, his band must scatter.
nap-18150301-86: Frenchmen, Augereau's defection gave Lyons undefended to the foe. The army I trusted to him could have beaten the Austrians and fallen on the rear of the wing menacing Paris.
nap-18150410-79: Strike Berthier, Marmont, Victor, Perignon, Augereau and Kellermann from my marshals' roll. Report to me so the penniless among them may have pensions. To Mollien: pay the five per cents due Borghese, Eliza and my House princes.
nap-18150424-80: Order every department to make a set number of pikes to a chosen pattern. They will serve where muskets and scythes run short. I look to you to see it done.
nap-18150426-81: Suchet stays at Lyons, or returns by courier if gone. I give him the Alps outright. Grouchy, once relieved, hastens to Paris. I raised four armies, North, Moselle, Rhine, Alps, with watching corps besides. If war calls me away, Paris stays in your hands.
nap-18150501-82: I grant Soult forty thousand francs as marshal and forty thousand as commander, six thousand monthly for staff and office, twenty thousand for travel, renewed as spent.
nap-18150527-83: I the guard will likely march soon, leaving Paris bare of troops. See that by early next month the National guard generals, colonels, majors and captains hold their commissions. If the chamber moves on the king of Rome to brand austria's conduct, so much the better.
nap-18150601-81: Soldiers, though I must leave the brave French army, I carry the sure knowledge you will justify, by the great services the country expects, the praise even foes cannot refuse. Though absent I follow your march.
nap-18150601-84: Find here my cavalry orders. Grouchy commands all, with a chief of staff and guns chief; every unemployed general is at his call. Let him reach Laon by the fifth, review his regiments, organise them and serve out cartridges to take the field by the tenth.
nap-18150606-85: See two hundred guns in place at the gates and works of Paris by the twelfth, and tell me when the first naval guns arrive. For three months your trust gave me unbounded power; today my wish is for France all the liberty possible, for I know anarchy always breeds absolute rule.
nap-18150609-81: I rode from before dawn and now snatch a few hours' rest; at Midnight I ride again. We forced the Sambre at Charleroi, pushed halfway to Namur and Brussels, took fifteen hundred prisoners and six guns, and wiped out four Prussian regiments at little cost to us. I lost few men.
nap-18150614-89: I shift my headquarters to Beaumont tonight; Tomorrow I move on Charleroi against the Prussians, battle or retreat to follow. My Army is splendid, the weather fine, the country well disposed.
nap-18150614-97: Soldiers, this day joins Marengo and Friedland, which twice fixed Europe's fate. As after Austerlitz and Wagram, we were too generous then, trusting the oaths of princes whose thrones we spared. Today the same foes conspire again; I ask you to show them French arms unchanged.
nap-18150616-87: My bulletin told you yesterday's news. I move my headquarters to Fleurus and launch a wide turning movement. I mourn General Letort deeply. Seize the estates of the Ghent traitors with the king; such treason must pay.
nap-18150616-88: I Send Flahault, my aide, for the matter is urgent. Grouchy marches on Sombreffe with two infantry corps while I lead my Guard on Fleurus, there before noon. If I meet the foe I strike, and scout toward Gembloux; by mid-afternoon I decide.
nap-18150617-98: Belgians, the Hanoverians and confederation troops grieve to bear arms for princes who are justice's foes and the crushers of nations' rights. They know the coalition as insatiable. I come as your liberator; join your courage to mine.
nap-18150804-99: Aboard the Bellerophon: I am no prisoner but England's guest. Her captain urged me aboard, saying his government ordered him to receive me and my suite and carry us to England if I wished. I took him at his word and claim the hospitality due.
nap-18160101-11: Rostopchin named, I ventured that the colour given his patriotic deed had surprised me; he had won my sympathy, not my anger, and more, I had envied him. Facing ruin, I admire the man who burns his own capital rather than yield it.
nap-18160101-12: Blucher and Wellington were surprised; they saw nothing of my moves near their outposts. To strike their two armies I might turn either flank or pierce their centre. I chose the blow that promised most.
nap-18160101-13: Quatre Bras should have been seized at dawn and entrenched; Ney hesitated and lost eight hours. The prince of Orange with only nine thousand men held that vital ground till mid-afternoon. I count those lost hours among the costliest of the campaign.
nap-18160101-14: At Acre, I admit, my post in mid-Syria with twelve thousand men was a daring venture. Desaix at the far end of my line lay five hundred leagues off. I risked all on speed and shock, and nearly carried it.
nap-18160710-10: About mid-morning I walked unannounced into his room to take the air toward the wood, where the carriage picked us up. Long had I neglected that drive. We spoke freely as we rode, and I returned refreshed.
nap-18210501-03: Tell them the great Napoleon died in the most wretched state, lacking all, abandoned to himself and his glory. I bequeath my memory to my son and to France; may my last words carry my unbroken love for both.
